customLessons.title: Human Body Systems (Circulatory and Nervous Systems)
objectives: Analyze the anatomy and physiology of the Circulatory System (four-chambered heart, vascular circuits, blood components) and Nervous System (CNS, PNS, reflex arc).
Conduct a pulse rate observation investigation comparing resting heart rate with post-exercise cardiovascular response.
Apply higher-order thinking to explain how the autonomic nervous system coordinates cardiovascular and respiratory adaptations during physical stress.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 6 SCIENCE — LESSON 1: Human Body Systems (Circulatory and Nervous Systems)
(Enhanced DepEd Curriculum — Revised Framework)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Explain how the organs of each system work together to coordinate bodily functions and respond to internal and external stimuli.

I. THE CIRCULATORY SYSTEM: THE BODY'S TRANSPORT HIGHWAY
• Four-Chambered Cardiovascular Pump:
  - Right Atrium & Ventricle: Collects deoxygenated blood from body tissues and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery.
  - Left Atrium & Ventricle: Muscular power chamber that receives freshly oxygenated blood from lungs and pumps it into the aorta to supply the entire body.
• Specialized Blood Vessels:
  - Arteries: Thick, elastic muscular walls carrying high-pressure blood away from the heart.
  - Veins: Thinner walls equipped with one-way pocket valves that prevent backflow of blood returning to the heart.
  - Capillaries: Microscopic single-cell-thick vessels where gas exchange (O2 / CO2) and nutrient delivery occur.
• Components of Blood: Red Blood Cells (hemoglobin carries oxygen), White Blood Cells (immune defense), Platelets (fibrin clot formation), and Plasma (92% water solvent transporting nutrients and hormones).

II. THE NERVOUS SYSTEM: MASTER COMMUNICATION GRID
• Central Nervous System (CNS): Brain (Cerebrum: thought/memory, Cerebellum: posture/coordination, Brainstem: breathing/heartbeat) and the Spinal Cord.
• Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): Sensory neurons (receptors to CNS) and Motor neurons (CNS to effector muscles).
• The Spinal Reflex Arc: An involuntary, lightning-fast protective circuit (e.g., pulling your hand away from a boiling kettle). Stimulus → Sensory Receptor → Sensory Neuron → Spinal Interneuron → Motor Neuron → Muscle Contraction. This survival arc bypasses the brain, acting before pain is consciously registered!

HANDS-ON OBSERVATION & INQUIRY TASK: The Cardiovascular Response to Exercise
1. Observation: Locate your radial pulse on the wrist. Count your beats for 60 seconds at rest. (Normal resting: 70–85 bpm).
2. Physical Stress Test: Perform 2 minutes of vigorous jumping jacks or running in place.
3. Immediate Measurement: Count your pulse rate immediately. Notice: Increased pulse (130–160 bpm), deeper breathing rate, flushed skin.
4. Explanation & HOTS Application:
   - Why did your pulse surge? Working leg muscles burned glucose and required massive oxygen delivery!
   - How did the body coordinate this? Sensory chemoreceptors detected rising CO2 in the blood; the brainstem activated the sympathetic autonomic nervous system, signaling the heart pacemaker (SA node) to pump faster and arteries to dilate!

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• The Circulatory System pumps blood in a double loop to deliver oxygen and nutrients.
• The Nervous System coordinates responses through voluntary brain pathways and rapid spinal reflex arcs.
• Observation and scientific measurement prove that organ systems dynamically adapt to support bodily exertion.

slides.title: Double Cardiovascular Circulation Loop

The Four-Chambered Marvel:
• Pulmonary Circuit: Right heart sends deoxygenated blood to lung alveoli for fresh O2
• Systemic Circuit: Left heart pumps high-pressure oxygen-rich blood through the aorta to all organs

slides.content:
Central Control and Emergency Reactions:
• Brain: Cerebrum (cognition), Cerebellum (balance/muscle coordination), Brainstem (involuntary survival)
• Spinal Reflex Arc: Sensory receptor -> Spinal cord interneuron -> Motor neuron -> Immediate muscle jerk!
• Emergency arcs protect your body before your brain registers pain!

customLessons.title: Reproduction in Plants
objectives: Differentiate sexual reproduction (pollination, fertilization, seed formation) from asexual reproduction in plants.
Explain and sequence artificial asexual propagation methods: cutting, budding, layering (marcotting), and grafting.
Analyze natural vegetative structures (runners, rhizomes, tubers, leaf plantlets) and evaluate agricultural advantages of clonal propagation.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 6 SCIENCE — LESSON 2: Reproduction in Plants
(Enhanced DepEd Curriculum — Sexual and Asexual Plant Propagation Suite)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Compare different modes of reproduction in plants (sexual vs. asexual) and explain how vegetative propagation techniques work.

I. SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN FLOWERING PLANTS
• Floral Organs: Stamen (male anther produces pollen grains; filament) and Pistil/Carpel (female sticky stigma, style, ovary with ovules).
• Pollination & Fertilization: Pollen transfers to stigma via wind or pollinators (bees, butterflies). A pollen tube grows down the style; male gametes fuse with the egg cell inside the ovule. The ovule develops into a SEED containing an embryo, and the ovary wall expands into a fleshy FRUIT.
• Benefit: Generates genetic variation, enabling seedlings to adapt to changing environmental conditions.

II. ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION: EXACT GENETIC CLONES
In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces offspring that are genetically identical to itself without seeds or fertilization.

FOUR MAJOR ARTIFICIAL PROPAGATION METHODS:
1. Stem Cutting:
   - Method: A healthy branch or shoot with vegetative nodes is cut and planted in moist soil or water.
   - Actual Plants: Sanseviera (Snake plant), Rose, Malunggay, Hibiscus (Gumamela), Sugarcane.
   - Mechanism: Undifferentiated meristematic cells at the stem nodes develop into adventitious roots.
2. Budding (T-Budding):
   - Method: A single vegetative bud (scion) is sliced from a desirable plant and inserted into a T-shaped slit in the bark of a hardy rootstock, then bound with grafting tape.
   - Actual Plants: Citrus (Calamansi, Orange), Roses, Rubber trees.
3. Layering / Marcotting (Air Layering):
   - Method: A 1-inch ring of bark is stripped from a mature branch (removing the phloem but leaving the xylem intact so water still reaches the tip). Moist sphagnum moss or coconut coir is wrapped around the wound and sealed in plastic wrap.
   - Actual Plants: Mango, Guava, Lanzones, Chico, Lemon.
   - Mechanism: Sugars traveling down from leaves accumulate at the cut bark, triggering rapid root sprouting. Once roots fill the wrap, the branch is sawed off and potted!
4. Grafting (Cleft/Whip Grafting):
   - Method: A scion twig with dormant buds from a high-quality mother tree is joined into a notched rootstock seedling. Crucial requirement: The green vascular cambium layers of both scion and rootstock must touch!
   - Actual Plants: Carabao Mango, Apple, Avocado, Coffee.

NATURAL VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION:
• Katakataka (Bryophyllum): Tiny complete plantlets sprout along the leaf margins and drop into soil.
• Tubers: Potato "eyes" sprout into new potato vines.
• Rhizomes: Horizontal underground stems in Ginger and Luya.
• Runners/Stolons: Creeping above-ground stems in Strawberry and Grass.

HOTS INQUIRY CHALLENGE: Why do Filipino Fruit Farmers Prefer Marcotting and Grafting over Planting Seeds?
1. Speed to Fruit: A grafted Carabao mango tree produces sweet fruit in 2 to 3 years, whereas a seed-grown tree takes 8 to 12 years!
2. True-to-Type Clones: Seeds result from cross-pollination and may produce sour, fibrous fruit. Grafting guarantees 100% exact genetic clones of sweet, prized fruit varieties!

slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 2: Life Science
(Enhanced DepEd Curriculum)

Explore plant reproduction: From floral pollination to cutting, budding, marcotting, and grafting.

slides.title: Sexual Reproduction: Flower to Fruit
slides.content:
The Pollination & Fertilization Journey:
• Male Stamen: Anther releases microscopic golden pollen grains
• Female Pistil: Stigma catches pollen -> Pollen tube grows down style
• Double Fertilization: Ovule becomes a fertile SEED; ovary ripens into a fleshy FRUIT!

slides.title: Asexual Methods: Cutting & Budding
slides.content:
Cloning Without Seeds:
• Stem Cutting: Nodal stem cuttings placed in moist soil generate adventitious roots (Sanseviera, Malunggay, Gumamela)
• Budding (T-Budding): Inserting a single bud from a superior scion into rootstock bark (Calamansi, Citrus, Roses)

slides.title: Sequencing: Marcotting & Grafting
slides.content:
Mastering Philippine Agricultural Techniques:
1. Marcotting (Air Layering): Strip 1-inch bark ring -> Wrap in moist coconut coir -> Wait for roots -> Cut and pot!
2. Grafting: Join scion twig into rootstock notch -> Align vascular cambium layers -> Bind tightly with tape -> Cells fuse into one tree!

Step 2: Strip bark ring (expose cambium)
Step 3: Pack with moist sphagnum moss
Step 4: Seal with plastic until roots sprout (Marcotting!)

customLessons.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
objectives: Classify animals into Vertebrates (with backbones) and Invertebrates (without backbones) and identify their distinguishing anatomical features.
Differentiate the 5 vertebrate classes (Fish, Amphibians, Reptiles, Birds, Mammals) and 5 major invertebrate phyla (Arthropods, Mollusks, Annelids, Cnidarians, Echinoderms).
Perform a hands-on classification activity observing Philippine animal specimen cards and justifying classification with anatomical evidence.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 6 SCIENCE — LESSON 3: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
(Enhanced DepEd Curriculum — Hands-on Classification & Performance Suite)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Classify animals into vertebrates and invertebrates based on anatomical characteristics, and explain the basis for their classification.

I. VERTEBRATES (CHORDATES): POSSESS AN INTERNAL BACKBONE
All vertebrates possess an internal endoskeleton with a spinal column supporting the body:
1. Fish: Aquatic, ectothermic, breathe with gills, covered in slimy scales, swim with fins (e.g., Bangus / Milkfish, Tilapia).
2. Amphibians: Ectothermic, dual life cycle (aquatic larvae breathe with gills; adults develop lungs and moist skin for gas exchange), lay jelly-like eggs in water (e.g., Philippine Bullfrog, Cane Toad).
3. Reptiles: Ectothermic, breathe exclusively with lungs, covered in dry keratinized scales, lay leathery-shelled eggs on land (e.g., Pawikan / Sea Turtle, Monitor Lizard / Bayawak, Cobra).
4. Birds (Aves): Endothermic (warm-blooded), feathers, lightweight hollow bones, toothless beaks, lay hard-shelled calcium eggs (e.g., Philippine Eagle, Maya Bird).
5. Mammals: Endothermic, have hair or fur, breathe with lungs, have mammary glands that produce milk to nurse young, give live birth (e.g., Philippine Tarsier, Carabao, Whale, Bat, Humans).

II. INVERTEBRATES: ANIMALS WITHOUT A BACKBONE (>95% OF ALL SPECIES)
• Arthropods: Largest phylum! Segmented bodies, jointed appendages, tough chitinous exoskeleton (e.g., Rhinoceros Beetle / Uwáng, Crabs, Spiders, Mosquitoes).
• Mollusks: Soft unsegmented bodies, muscular foot, visceral mass, often enclosed in hard calcium carbonate shells (e.g., Giant Clam / Taklobo, Snails, Squids).
• Annelids: Segmented cylindrical worm bodies with hydrostatic skeletons (e.g., Earthworms / Bulate, Leeches).
• Cnidarians: Radial symmetry, gelatinous body, tentacles armed with stinging cnidocyte capsules (e.g., Box Jellyfish, Sea Anemones, Coral polyps).
• Echinoderms: Spiny skin, five-part radial symmetry, marine water vascular system with tube feet (e.g., Starfish, Sea Urchins, Sea Cucumbers / Balatan).

HANDS-ON PERFORMANCE TASK: Philippine Specimen Classification & Justification
Learners inspect 8 Philippine animal cards and complete the scientific classification log:
1. Philippine Tarsier → Vertebrate (Mammal): Has internal spinal column, fur, and nurses young with milk.
2. Milkfish (Bangus) → Vertebrate (Fish): Has internal spine, gills, and paired swimming fins.
3. Rhinoceros Beetle (Uwáng) → Invertebrate (Arthropod): Lacks internal backbone; protected by jointed chitinous exoskeleton.
4. Giant Clam (Taklobo) → Invertebrate (Mollusk): Soft body protected by a two-valved calcium carbonate shell, no backbone.
5. Sea Turtle (Pawikan) → Vertebrate (Reptile): Internal bony skeleton, lungs, dry scaly skin, leathery eggs.
6. Box Jellyfish → Invertebrate (Cnidarian): Soft gelatinous body with stinging tentacles and no spine.
7. Maya Bird → Vertebrate (Bird): Internal vertebral skeleton, hollow bones, and feather covering.
8. Earthworm (Bulate) → Invertebrate (Annelid): Segmented cylindrical ringed body with no vertebrae.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Vertebrates have backbones (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals).
• Invertebrates have no backbones (arthropods, mollusks, annelids, cnidarians, echinoderms).
• Classification must be justified using observable anatomical evidence.

slides.title: The Five Vertebrate Classes
slides.content:
Internal Bony Skeletons & Spinal Columns:
• Fish: Gills, scales, fins, cold-blooded (Bangus)
• Amphibians: Moist skin, water-land metamorphosis (Frogs)
• Reptiles: Dry scales, lungs, leathery eggs (Pawikan, Monitor lizard)
• Birds: Feathers, hollow flight bones, warm-blooded (Philippine Eagle)
• Mammals: Hair/fur, mammary glands nursing young (Tarsier, Carabao)

slides.title: Major Invertebrate Phyla (>95% of Species)
slides.content:
Creatures Without Backbones:
• Arthropods: Jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton (Uwáng beetle, crabs)
• Mollusks: Soft unsegmented bodies, calcium shells (Taklobo giant clam)
• Annelids: Segmented rings, hydrostatic skeleton (Earthworms)
• Cnidarians: Stinging tentacles, radial symmetry (Jellyfish, corals)
• Echinoderms: Spiny skin, tube feet (Starfish, sea urchins)

customLessons.title: Ecosystem Relationships (Food Webs, Interaction Among Living Things, Biotic and Abiotic Factors in an Ecosystem)
objectives: Analyze interconnected food webs and evaluate trophic cascades triggered by human disruptions.
Differentiate symbiotic relationships (Mutualism, Commensalism, Parasitism, Predation, Competition) in Philippine ecosystems.
Apply ecological concepts to practical real-world situations: mangrove conservation, reef restoration, and community biodiversity projects.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 6 SCIENCE — LESSON 4: Ecosystem Relationships
(Enhanced DepEd Curriculum — Real-World Practical Situations Suite)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Describe the interactions among living things and their physical environment in diverse Philippine ecosystems and propose responsible actions to conserve biodiversity.

I. BIOTIC AND ABIOTIC DYNAMICS
• Biotic Factors (Living Components): Plants, animals, fungi, and decomposing bacteria.
• Abiotic Factors (Physical Environment): Sunlight intensity, ambient temperature, water salinity, soil pH, dissolved oxygen, and mineral nutrients.
• Constant Balance: Changing an abiotic factor (e.g. warming ocean water) directly affects biotic life (e.g. coral bleaching).

II. FOOD WEBS & TROPHIC STABILITY
• Natural ecosystems are not isolated food chains, but interwoven FOOD WEBS.
• Animals have diverse food sources: If one prey species declines, predators consume alternatives.
• Keystone Species: Predators (e.g., Reef Sharks, Philippine Eagles) keep herbivore populations balanced, preventing them from overconsuming the plant base.

III. FIVE SYMBIOTIC RELATIONSHIPS IN PHILIPPINE NATURE:
1. Mutualism (+ / +): Both species benefit.
   - Example: Coral polyps and photosynthetic zooxanthellae algae; Bees pollinating coffee blossoms while harvesting nectar.
2. Commensalism (+ / 0): One benefits, other is unaffected.
   - Example: Aerial orchids rooted on high bark of Narra trees to reach sunlight without drawing tree sap.
3. Parasitism (+ / -): Parasite extracts nutrients at host's expense.
   - Example: Mosquitoes transmitting dengue virus, intestinal roundworms in livestock.
4. Predation (+ / -): Predator captures and consumes prey.
   - Example: Philippine Eagle preying on monkeys and monitor lizards.
5. Competition (- / -): Organisms compete for limited resources (light, water, nesting territory).

IV. THREE PRACTICAL REAL-WORLD SITUATIONS FOR GRADE 6:
• Situation 1: Mangrove Ecosystem Protection in Laguna/Batangas Coastlines
  - Problem: Cutting down bakawan (mangroves) for coastal developments destroys juvenile fish nurseries and leaves coastal barangays defenseless against typhoon storm surges.
  - Practical Action: Community reforestation of Rhizophora mangrove propagules along tidal mudflats restores fish breeding grounds and stabilizes coastlines.
• Situation 2: The Coral Reef Trophic Cascade
  - Problem: Illegal blast fishing and cyanide harvesting decimate predatory grouper and snapper fish.
  - Trophic Consequence: Crown-of-thorns starfish and sea urchins multiply unchecked, devouring living coral heads and turning vibrant reefs into dead rubble.
  - Practical Action: Establishing Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) where fishing is strictly prohibited lets reef fish populations recover and restore ecological equilibrium.
• Situation 3: Designing a School Native Pollinator Garden
  - Practical Action: Grade 6 pupils establish a dedicated school biodiversity sanctuary planting endemic flowering shrubs to support native honeybees and butterfly pollinators.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Food webs provide ecological stability through multi-pathway energy networks.
• Symbiotic relationships govern species interactions (mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, predation, competition).
• Practical human interventions (mangrove planting, marine reserves, pollinator gardens) restore ecosystem health.

slides.title: Biotic & Abiotic Interactions
slides.content:
The Living and Physical Worlds Intertwined:
• Biotic Factors: Producers, herbivores, predators, fungi, soil microbes
• Abiotic Factors: Sunlight, temperature, rainfall, dissolved oxygen, salinity
• Healthy ecosystems require balance between physical conditions and living communities!

slides.title: The Five Symbiotic Relationships
slides.content:
How Organisms Live Together:
• Mutualism (+ / +): Both benefit (Corals & algae; Bees & flowers)
• Commensalism (+ / 0): One benefits, other unharmed (Orchids on Narra bark)
• Parasitism (+ / -): Parasite harms host (Ticks, intestinal worms)
• Predation (+ / -): Hunter catches prey
• Competition (- / -): Fighting for limited food or territory

Real-World Philippine Application:

• Planting native mangrove propagules along muddy coastlines protects barangays from typhoons and restores fisheries
• Practical science drives community resilience!
